prize_parts.citation: for the development of ionizable lipid nanoparticles, based on pH-dependent lipid chemistry and controlled self-assembly, that deliver nucleic-acid medicines into cells

statement.case_for: After the full exchange I still rank ionizable lipid nanoparticles first, and I now make the case on a narrower and, I think, more defensible footing. The decisive chemical insight is a lipid whose charge is switched by pH: neutral in circulation, cationic in the acidic endosome, where it destabilises the membrane and releases the cargo, combined with the self-assembly of nucleic acid and lipid by rapid mixing into small, reproducible particles. That is molecular design with a measurable mechanism, it was replicated and extended by many groups, and it is the delivery vehicle in approved siRNA therapy and in mRNA vaccines given to billions of people. Round 1 showed that no shortlisted alternative combines this level of demonstrated consequence with a mechanism that is clearly chemical. I have therefore moved from Cullis and Langer to Cullis, Hope and Madden, the Vancouver line in which ionizable lipids and rapid-mixing formulation were developed. The citation is written around that mechanism, not around delivery in general, which also keeps it distinct from the 2023 Medicine prize for nucleoside modification.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the weak point. The cut excludes Langer and Anderson, whose lipidoid and combinatorial work made the idea general, and MacLachlan, whose group delivered the first clinically validated siRNA formulation; part of the decisive formulation work was done in companies and is partly proprietary. The Medicine prize of 2023 makes a delivery-vehicle award look adjacent to the public, even if the science is different. I am also aware that I came in sympathetic to translational chemistry, and I tried to test the case against the maturity standard I apply to PROTACs and perovskites rather than only against my own interests. Finally, the committee has to decide whether a trio of three colleagues from one laboratory is the right shape for a prize that is about a technology many groups built.

responses.point: Sparr argued that the decisive chemistry is pH-dependent ionizable lipids, lipid polymorphism and rapid-mixing self-assembly, which trace to Cullis, Hope and Madden, and that pairing Cullis with Langer credits a broader delivery concept than the lipid physical chemistry.
responses.response: You moved me on this. In round 1 I defended Langer as the person who made delivery general, but your point is that the prize should reward one mechanism and not a family of strategies. Lipid polymorphism, the pKa-tuned headgroup and endosomal escape are what a chemist can state in one sentence, and they belong to the Vancouver group. I have adopted your trio. What I still ask of you is whether you accept the lipidoid line as supportive, not decisive, because if you think it is decisive the trio cannot hold, and I would like us to find that out before the ballot. I also share your caution about the 2023 prize and have addressed it in the citation.

responses.point: Aqvist said a fair three-name prize needs a defensible decisive step and that he could not yet say who holds it for lipid nanoparticles; he also asked Sparr whether Cullis, Hope and Madden is the right cut.
responses.response: Johan's test is the right one, and my answer is the combination of an ionizable, pH-switched lipid and rapid-mixing assembly, which gave small, stable particles that could be made reproducibly. That step is what the approved siRNA and mRNA products inherit, whereas lipidoid screening broadened the choice of lipids. On Car-Parrinello, I still have not seen a result outside theory that depends on the fictitious-dynamics formulation as distinct from Born-Oppenheimer dynamics, and I think the 1998 and 2013 prizes make it harder to argue a third computational award, but I respect that the attribution is the tidiest on the list.

responses.point: Linke ranked halide perovskites first, arguing the prize concerns the discovery of the absorber and a decade of replication, not product deployment, while naming Miyasaka, Park and Snaith with Gratzel, Seok and Kanatzidis left out.
responses.response: Heiner, I accept your distinction between a discovery and a product, and it weakens my objection that no perovskite module is deployed. My remaining concern is different: the committee itself says the cut leaves out Gratzel, Seok and Kanatzidis, and that device engineering may place the work in physics. That is the same type of attribution problem I have with lipid nanoparticles, but here with a stability question also open. If the committee prefers B016, I could support the trio, and I have listed it among my alternatives for that reason. I still think the lipid case offers more demonstrated consequence at similar attribution risk.

responses.point: Zou argued that delivery was built from liposome work, lipidoid screening and industrial formulation by many groups and that the 2023 Medicine prize already covers the mRNA vaccine story, so the chemistry-specific claim of Cullis, Hope and Madden needs careful argument.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge, and the revised citation is my attempt to answer it. The 2023 prize recognised the modified nucleoside that made mRNA tolerable to the immune system; it did not recognise the vehicle that gets it into the cytosol, and siRNA medicines, which have nothing to do with nucleoside modification, depend on the same lipids. I agree that liposome work preceded the Vancouver group, but ionizable lipids that are inert at neutral pH and active in the endosome are a distinct step. I would ask whether you would support a cut around that step, since your own ranking placed perovskites ahead mainly on cleaner attribution.

uncertainties: Whether Cullis, Hope and Madden are indeed the holders of the decisive ionizable-lipid and rapid-mixing step, or whether MacLachlan, Anderson or Langer should displace one; I rely on recalled history and have not verified priority details.
Whether a delivery-vehicle prize will be read as too close to the 2023 Medicine prize despite the different mechanism.
Whether any single configuration can reach five votes; B016 is the only one with more than one explicit supporter, and I could accept it as a fallback.
How much clinical maturity should count against PROTACs and commercial deployment against perovskites, given that I apply it asymmetrically in favour of lipid nanoparticles.
statement.conflict_note: No change in my disclosure. I have no known connection to the Vancouver, MIT or Alnylam groups or to any credited person. My translational and biomaterials interests, and my biosensor start-up experience, make me sympathetic to delivery technologies, and I have tried to test the case on chemistry and attribution rather than on impact alone. No recusal is sought.
